props.title: What Lies Beneath

sections.content: What Lies Beneath (2000) marked Robert Zemeckis's foray into Hitchcockian suspense, crafting a supernatural thriller that plays like a modern take on Vertigo (1958) and Rebecca (1940). Michelle Pfeiffer delivers a masterfully paranoid performance as Claire Spencer, a woman who becomes convinced her neighbor's ghost is haunting her lakeside home. The film cleverly subverts expectations - what begins as a straightforward ghost story evolves into a complex psychological thriller about marriage, betrayal, and buried secrets. Zemeckis employs his technical expertise to create unbearable tension, particularly in the film's infamous bathtub sequence.

sections.content: The film belongs to a specific late 90s/early 2000s wave of supernatural thrillers that merged domestic drama with horror elements. Like The Sixth Sense (1999) and The Others (2001), it relies heavily on atmosphere and slow-burning tension rather than jump scares. Harrison Ford plays against type as Norman Spencer, bringing subtle menace to what could have been a standard supportive husband role. The film's greatest strength is how it uses its ghost story framework to explore themes of marital trust and female intuition. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation in Supernatural Thrillers

Zemeckis applies the technical innovation he's known for (Back to the Future (1985), Contact (1997)) to create some of the most effective supernatural sequences of the era. The mirror scenes and underwater shots influenced later ghost stories like The Conjuring (2013) and Insidious (2010). The film's use of reflective surfaces and negative space to create tension became a template for modern horror cinematography.
